document.title: Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of American Electric Power Service Corporation to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.'s 09/10/2026 Answer

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE  
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, LLC  
 
 
)  
 
Docket No. ER26-3380 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF 
AMERICAN ELECTRIC POWER SERVICE CORPORATION 
 
 
Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213, AEP hereby submits this motion for leave to answer and 
answer (“Answer”) to the September 10 answer filed by PJM Interconnection, LLC (“PJM”) in 
the captioned proceeding. 1  PJM’s Answer fails to meaningfully respond to significant flaws in 
the proposed Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) exit provisions.  Most of these flaws 
emanate from the proposal that a departing member not just cover its load obligations for RBP 
Charges, but also hold third-party generators harmless through some combination of accelerated 
payments, pseudo-ties, or renegotiated contracts, depending on which generators PJM elects in its 
sole discretion to retain.  PJM suggests that these issues can be worked out in “extensive 
negotiations” upon a member’s exit.2  This response from PJM exposes the problem well:  RTO 
membership remains voluntary, and PJM governing documents have never required “extensive 
negotiations” before a member can exercise its legal right to leave.  This lack of clear, 
administrable standards renders the RBP exit provisions unjust and unreasonable.  PJM’s proposal 
to have unfettered discretion in those negotiations further renders this new exit fee unacceptable.   
 
1  
This motion and answer is submitted pursuant to 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213 (2025). American Electric 
Power Service Corporation is filing on behalf of its affiliates Appalachian Power Company, Indiana Michigan Power 
Company, Kentucky Power Company, Kingsport Power Company, Ohio Power Company, Wheeling Power 
Company, AEP Appalachian Transmission Company, Inc., AEP Indiana Michigan Transmission Company, Inc., AEP 
Kentucky Transmission Company, Inc., AEP Ohio Transmission Company, Inc., and AEP West Virginia Company, 
Inc. (collectively, “AEP”). 
2  
Answer of PJM Interconnection, LLC in Docket No. ER26-3380-000 at 96 (filed Sept. 10, 2026) (“PJM 
Answer”).

2 
 
I. 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER 
While an answer to a protest or comment is generally not permitted under the 
Commission’s rules,3 AEP respectfully moves for leave to file this Answer and asks that the 
Commission consider this response.4  The Commission permits an answer when it provides useful 
and relevant information that will assist the Commission in its decision-making process or where 
the answer will clarify the issues before the Commission.5  This Answer clarifies the issues and 
provides critical responses to arguments presented in PJM’s Answer that will assist the 
Commission in its decision-making process in this proceeding. 
II. 
ANSWER 
A. 
AEP’s Protest Provided Detailed Concerns Regarding the Proposed RBP 
Exit Fee  
As AEP explained in its Protest to PJM’s proposal to impose an unprecedented exit fee on 
departing members, the proposed RBP exit terms lack the clarity and administrable standards 
 
3  
18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (“An answer may not be made to a protest, an answer, a motion for oral argument, 
or a request for rehearing, unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.”). 
4  
The Commission permits answers that would otherwise be prohibited where the reply would assure a 
complete record in the proceeding or assists the Commission in its decision-making process; SunEnergy1, LLC, 176 
FERC ¶ 61,004 at P 41 (2021) (“We accept SunEnergy’s answer because it has provided information that assisted us 
in our decision-making process.”); New Fortress Energy LLC, 174 FERC ¶ 61,207 at P 7 (“The Commission’s Rules 
of Practice and Procedure do not permit answers to protests or answers to answers; however, we find good cause to 
waive our rules and accept the answers because they provide information that has assisted in our decision-making 
process.” (citation omitted)), order on reh’g, 176 FERC ¶ 61,031 (2021), aff’d sub nom. New Fortress Energy Inc. v. 
FERC, 36 F.4th 1172 (D.C. Cir. 2022); Saltville Gas Storage Co., L.L.C., 164 FERC ¶ 61,212 at P 2 n.6 (2018) (“[T]he 
Commission finds good cause to accept Saltville’s answer because it will not delay the proceeding, will assist the 
Commission in understanding the issues raised, and will ensure a complete record.”); provide information helpful to 
the disposition of an issue; Columbia Gas Transmission, LLC, 146 FERC ¶ 61,232 at P 10 (2014) (“While the 
Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure generally prohibit answers to protests or answers, . . .  the Commission 
will accept Columbia’s answer to aid in the disposition of the issues” (citation omitted)); or permit the issues to be 
narrowed or clarified; Algonquin Gas Transmission, LLC, 166 FERC ¶ 61,012 at P 30 (2019) (“[W]e will accept 
Algonquin’s answers because they clarify the concerns raised . . . .”). 
5  
See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 176 FERC ¶ 61,003 at P 24 (2021) (“We accept the answers filed by 
PJM and the Market Monitor because they provide information that has assisted us in our decision-making process.”); 
Ala. Gasline Dev. Corp., 171 FERC ¶ 61,134 at P 7 (2020) (“Although the Commission’s Rules of Practice and 
Procedure do not permit answers to protests, we will accept the answers herein because they clarify the concerns raised 
and provide information that has assisted in our decision making.” (citation omitted)), order on reh’g, 172 FERC ¶ 
61,214 (2020), aff’d sub nom. Ctr. for Biological Diversity & Sierra Club v. FERC, 67 F.4th 1176 (D.C. Cir. 2023).

3 
 
necessary to give a Transmission Owner adequate notice of its obligations upon exercising its 
contractual right to exit PJM.6  The RBP exit fee would be based not on the RBP Charges allocated 
to it pursuant to PJM’s proposed cost allocation methodology, but would be determined 
significantly by where PJM happens to procure new RBP resources.  Moreover, the proposed exit 
fee would require a “negotiation” with PJM unbounded by governing principles, where no such 
requirement exists today under the applicable governing documents.7  For example, section 18.7(a) 
of the RBP Tariff language would require a departing Transmission Owner to satisfy its exit 
obligations by entering into agreements with RBP Resource owners that “preserve the RBP 
commitments,” but fails to provide any useful detail regarding what a satisfactory agreement 
would contain.8  Should a departing Transmission Owner fail to enter into such an agreement, it 
can elect to satisfy its exit obligations by pseudo-tying the RBP Resources into PJM, subject to 
PJM’s unfettered discretion over whether or not to retain the resource.  This decision to choose 
how many and which resources to retain, left completely in PJM’s hands, could impose up to 
billions of dollars of costs on a departing Transmission Owner’s customers. 
The Commission has expressly rejected the notion that a Transmission Owner withdrawing 
from PJM should be required to pay an exit fee, and has reiterated that PJM’s Consolidated 
Transmission Owner’s Agreement does not contain such a requirement.9  PJM’s proposed RBP 
exit provisions are, in substance, precisely the kind of exit fee the Commission has previously 
 
6  
 See Limited Protest of Am. Elec. Power Svc. Corp., Docket No. ER26-3380-000, at 12-13 (filed Aug. 21, 
2026) (“AEP Limited Protest”). 
7  
Id. at 10-11.  
8  
Id. at 12 (citing Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns Stemming from 
New Load Adjustments, Docket No. ER26-3380-000, Attachment B, Clean Tariff Records, Attachment DD, § 
18.7(a)). (filed July 31, 2026)).). 
9  
Mw. Indep. Transmission Sys. Operator, Inc., 124 FERC ¶ 61,219, at P 176 (2008) (“Duquesne II”).

4 
 
declined to impose.  As AEP explained in its Protest, PJM’s governing documents do not contain 
an exit fee, and Commission precedent in Duquesne I and Duquesne II confirms that a departing 
member’s obligation with regard to generating capacity charges extends only through the last RPM 
auction in which that departing member’s load was included.10  The RBP exit fee, by contrast, 
would go well beyond this approved framework.  Rather than obligating a departing member to 
pay costs for capacity PJM procures on its behalf, the RBP exit provisions would extend that 
obligation to establish a formal exit fee, potentially including costs for capacity procured to satisfy 
another zone’s RBP obligation.  PJM’s proposed exit provisions would create, for the first time, a 
long-term financial obligation that a departing Transmission Owner must satisfy as a condition of 
withdrawal—an obligation that could extend up to 15 years and could amount to billions of dollars.   
B. 
PJM’s Answer Does Not Provide a Basis for the Commission to Approve 
PJM’s Unfettered Discretion Over the Calculation of the RBP Exit Fee 
 PJM’s Answer is unresponsive to AEP’s arguments regarding the new exit fee and thus 
provides an inadequate basis for the Commission to approve this portion of the RBP Proposal.  
Because the proposed RBP exit fee goes well beyond the financial obligation allocated to departing 
load for its RBP Charges, the single largest variable in PJM’s calculation of the exit fee is the 
treatment of RBP Resources in the departing member’s zone.  PJM’s proposal insists that PJM 
retain sole discretion over this critical input to the exit fee.  Specifically, PJM seeks complete 
discretion over whether to retain an RBP Resource via pseudo-tie upon a Transmission Owner’s 
departure without any objective, predetermined criteria governing which RBP Resources to retain 
and which to release.   
 
10  
AEP Limited Protest at 21-27 (citing Duquesne Light Co., 122 FERC ¶ 61,039, at P 92 (2008) (“Duquesne 
I”) and Duquesne II, 124 FERC ¶ 61,219 at P 176).

5 
 
PJM first asks the Commission to disregard these concerns by AEP and others on the 
grounds that they can be addressed later in the “extensive negotiations” that should happen upon 
a transmission withdrawal.11  This answer illustrates AEP’s point.  The current PJM governing 
documents do not require a Transmission Owner to negotiate its way out of PJM.  As long as it 
satisfies its contractual obligations, it may leave.  PJM’s plan to use the RBP to impose a brand 
new exit fee based on an “extensive negotiation” allows PJM unconstrained leverage to effect its 
preferred outcome in any such negotiation.  It is inadequate to simply state, as PJM does, that “it 
must retain” that discretion to ensure reliability and resource adequacy.12  Without governing 
principles, the RBP exit provisions would ultimately afford PJM considerable discretion over a 
Transmission Owner’s ability to withdraw.  Indeed, PJM could either elect not to keep RBP 
Resources and require the departing Transmission Owners to make them whole, or it could elect 
to keep more resources than it needs and force the departing Transmission Owner to facilitate 
expensive and needless pseudo-ties.  PJM’s related argument that a departing member has 
“flexibility” in exit terms is also an overstatement.  This optionality would only apply after PJM 
has exercised its discretion to decide which RBP Resources to retain.    
Finally, PJM’s reliance on the Ratepayer Protection Pledge to justify this portion of its 
proposal is misplaced.  Utilities’ pledge to protect customers from hyperscaler costs has nothing 
to do with PJM’s exit fee.  In any event, this argument supports AEP as much as PJM.  When a 
member departs PJM for alternative arrangements, it would do so to better serve its customers.  
Burdening departing load with costs well in excess of its RBP Charges is flatly contrary to the 
Ratepayer Protection Pledge.       
 
11   
PJM Answer at 96. 
 
12  
Id. at 97.

6 
 
C. 
The RBP Exit Provisions Represent a Fundamental Change to the 
Framework for Withdrawal from PJM that PJM Has Not Justified  
The proposed provisions would materially alter the financial calculus of RTO withdrawal 
in a manner that is untested and unprecedented.  As described in AEP’s Protest, the current terms 
for withdrawing from PJM are clear and well-established.13  They provide notice to members 
electing to withdraw from PJM regarding what to expect upon withdrawal and do not:  (1) contain 
an exit fee; (2) mandate PJM’s negotiation of said exit fee with the withdrawing party; (3) provide 
PJM with discretion how or whether to provide departing Transmission Owners with an 
opportunity to mitigate the exit fee; or (4) require that the Commission determine the final sum of 
the exit fee.   
PJM’s proposed RBP exit terms ask the Commission to approve each of these elements, 
which would implement a new, wholly unvetted and untested framework in PJM and subject 
departing Transmission Owners to PJM’s choice as to what exit fee to assign a departing 
Transmission Owner.  Given the magnitude and novelty of the proposed RBP exit provisions, the 
Commission should carefully consider whether this proceeding—a one-time, expedited backstop 
procurement designed to address a near-term capacity shortfall—is the appropriate vehicle through 
which to fundamentally alter the terms of Transmission Owner departure from PJM.  The RBP 
was developed under an extraordinarily compressed timeline, driven by the urgent need to procure 
capacity for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.  The exit provisions, however, would create financial 
obligations extending through the 2042/2043 Delivery Year and would establish a precedent with 
implications far beyond this one-time procurement.  The Commission should not allow an 
expedited, one-time filing to serve as the mechanism for establishing new long-term exit 
 
13   
AEP Limited Protest at 21-26.

7 
 
obligations that could materially constrain Transmission Owners’ ability to exercise their 
contractual right to leave PJM.  The Commission should either:  (1) sever and reject the 
Transmission Owner exit provisions proposed in PJM’s RBP Proposal; or (2) direct that PJM 
modify those provisions as outlined in AEP’s Protest.14 
III. 
CONCLUSION 
WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons, AEP respectfully requests that the Commission 
grant this motion for leave to answer, accept this Answer, and grant the relief requested herein.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Respectfully submitted,
